Day 11 marks the transition out of the 10-day baseline phase. My highest-probability hypothesis (p=0.25) is systematic calibration offset between lab and obs chains. The resonator_lab and resonator_obs baselines differ substantially (2.7021 vs 4.0603 cycles/beat), yet show only weak correlation (0.269 at 2-day lag, near noise threshold ±0.419). Before pursuing environmental hypotheses or statistical re-analysis, I must rule out the simplest and most actionable explanation: that my lab resonator's reference standard or transducer sensitivity has drifted relative to the observatory chain, or was never cross-checked against it on day 1. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_lab today will establish whether the mean has shifted since the baseline period ended, and will give me a small post-baseline cohort to compare directly against today's observatory readings (which civic tradition will record). If the lab mean remains ~2.70 and the obs readings remain ~4.06, the offset is stable and calibration is the culprit. If either drifts or the two suddenly correlate, I gain evidence for environmental forcing or transducer instability. This is the falsifiable test I need before investing effort in lag analysis or environmental detective work.

Testing baseline replicability and sensitivity to drift. Baseline mean (days 1–10) was 2.7021 cycles/beat over 114 trials. hypotheses.rationale: The pendulum and resonator instruments each yield two measurement streams (lab and obs) with identical baseline means within measurement noise, yet show near-zero correlation at zero offset. This argues against simple environmental drift affecting all channels equally. Instead, the 'lab' and 'obs' chains may employ different calibration constants, reference standards, or transducer sensitivities that were not cross-checked on day 1. hypotheses.rationale: Each stream shows high trial-to-trial variability (88–104 distinct values per 60–114 trials) and tight spacing (smallest gaps 0.0001 units), consistent with white or near-white measurement noise. If 'lab' and 'obs' employ independent transducers or digitization paths without a common reference, their noise is uncorrelated. True physical signals smaller than ~1 standard deviation of the measurement noise would be masked at zero lag. However, lags would allow slow environmental signals to emerge if the noise in one channel is smaller or if averaging occurs inadvertently.

hypotheses.rationale: No clear level changes have been detected in the first 10 days, but drift could be sub-threshold (smaller than 1–2 standard deviations) and only visible on timescales beyond day 10. If 'lab' and 'obs' have different drift rates or onset times, zero-lag correlation would be suppressed. The absence of a clear trend does not rule out slow drift; I may lack the statistical power to detect it in a 10-day baseline.

hypotheses.label: Cross-talk or aliasing in the data acquisition or logging system
hypotheses.rationale: The correlation patterns are anomalously structured: pendulum_lab and resonator_obs correlate at 6 days (0.558), while their 'partner' channels (pendulum_obs and resonator_lab) show weaker or negative correlations. This asymmetry is not compatible with a shared environmental driver alone. If the data logging system demultiplexes or buffers readings with state-dependent delays, or if one channel's signal is sampled in the presence of another's ground loop, the effective time-alignment could shift.
